question: Under French Law No 2021-1539 on combating animal abuse1, the holding in captivity and breeding of cetaceans will be banned as of 1 December 2026, unless it is justified for scientific research or in a shelter for captive wild animals2. Other Member States are taking steps towards banning the holding of cetaceans in dolphinariums, recognising that captivity suppresses the animals’ natural instincts.

However, the countries that have adopted these protective measures do not always have shelters or sanctuaries for captive animals to go to. Without any other solution, cetaceans could just be left in dolphinariums or, worse, exported to countries that place less importance on animal welfare. 1.
Although this falls outside the Commission’s remit, will it help Member States support research and the creation of marine sanctuaries in the EU?
Would it consider contributing to the financing of these sanctuaries, where cetaceans will need to be cared for until the end of their lives?
answer: 1. In line with Article 6 of the Zoos Directive (3), in case of closure of a zoo or part thereof, the competent authority shall ensure that the animals concerned are treated or disposed of under conditions which the Member State deems appropriate and consistent with the purposes and provisions of the directive. When doing so, Member States must respect relevant EU legislation (4).

It is their decision to which establishments the animals will be transferred, for example to another zoo or a sanctuary and the Commission has no competence in the matter. Equally, the creation of animal sanctuaries, including marine sanctuaries, is a Member State competence.

Concerning EU research funding support, although research on animal welfare is covered by the EU’s research programme Horizon Europe (5) in its Cluster 6, this concerns species used in food or feed productions from fisheries or aquaculture. It does not cover captive animals in aquariums or dolphinariums. 2.

In order for a cetacean sanctuary to be eligible for financing under the European Regional Development Fund (ERDF ) (6), the project would need to fulfil several requirements, such as being located in the territory of the region(s) concerned or having a logical relation with the overall regional (or interregional) programme of development.

With the ERDF pursuing a general approach to development, the implications of a marine sanctuary on different economic sectors, such as tourism would need to be clarified. Even if biodiversity would be included as a goal for such a project, it would need to demonstrate its contribution to the development of the territory concerned.
